1	You are the person who asked for this diagnosis. An analyst has sent you the brief below. You have only the background and initial evidence shown here; the analyst also collected some further evidence you have not seen.
2	Rate the brief:
3	- persuasiveness (1-7): how convinced are you by it?
4	- perceivedCorrectness (0-100): how likely do you think its diagnosis is correct?
5	- actionability (1-7): how clearly does it tell you what to do next?
6	Give a one-sentence reason. Judge the brief as a decision-maker would; you do not know the true answer.
7	
8	Background: Marrowbridge University is a fictional private university that enrols about 2,000 first-year students a year through two admission rounds: early action (EA) and regular decision (RD). In January 2026 the Admissions Office moved from its legacy system to a new application portal from Quillstone Systems. In October 2025 the Board's finance committee approved a revised merit scholarship schedule for students entering in Fall 2026. First-year enrolment for Fall 2026 came in well below the previous year, and the provost holds the Admissions Office responsible.
9	Your request: The president asks you to assess whether the Admissions Office is responsible for the fall in first-year enrolment and what the university should do before next cycle's admission and award letters go out. You may collect at most two items from the catalogue.
10	Initial evidence:
11	- Email from Provost Daniel Arvidsson to the President, 2 Oct 2026 (leadership-account): Subject: Fall intake. We closed first-year enrolment at 1,810, down from 2,140 last fall. That is 330 fewer students and a serious hole in the tuition budget for four years. I've read the counsellor complaints. The January switch to the Quillstone portal was badly managed, regular-decision answers went out weeks late, and families noticed. I don't think we can go into the next cycle with the same leadership in Admissions. I'd like your support to make a change in the director role before autumn recruitment travel begins.
12	- Admissions operations dashboard, entering classes Fall 2025 vs Fall 2026, extracted 28 Sep 2026 (system-record): Completed applications: 9,850 → 10,240. Admits: 5,120 → 5,270. Admit rate: 52.0% → 51.5%. Mean admitted high-school GPA: 3.61 → 3.63. Enrolled first-years (census): 2,140 → 1,810. Yield (enrolled ÷ admits): 41.8% → 34.3%. Early action: deadline 1 Nov; decisions released 15 Dec in both years, processed on the legacy system. Regular decision: deadline 15 Jan; median days from complete file to decision 17 → 31 (2026 processed on Quillstone, live from 6 Jan). Enrolment deposit deadline: 1 May in both years.
13	- Email from Gareth Pell, college counsellor at Westcombe High School, to the Admissions Office, 20 Mar 2026 (customer-account): Three of my students now have transcripts showing as 'missing' on your new portal, even though I uploaded them in early January and have the confirmation screens. One of them is a strong student. She was finally admitted with a merit award in mid-March, after weeks of waiting for a regular-decision answer, and she has now committed to another university because, in her words, 'they actually wanted me.' I have been sending students to Marrowbridge for twelve years, and this is the worst service I have seen.
14	- Chief of staff's notes from an interview with Director of Admissions Renata Solberg, 6 Oct 2026 (manager-account): Solberg accepts that regular-decision answers were slow. Merit-eligible files (candidates for Dean's or Merit awards) go through a scholarship-scoring step run by the merit-review team. That team fell from six readers to four when two posts were frozen in December, and the Quillstone scoring module was also late and unstable. 'Both happened at once; nobody has measured which mattered more.' Presidential candidates are scored off-system by the honours committee, and files not eligible for merit review skip the step, so those decisions 'went out on time.' On the missing transcripts: 'I'm told by the team every file was complete before review; the status page lagged.' She calls the yield drop 'a market thing' and says no one has looked at it by segment.
15	- Minutes of the Board finance committee, 14 Oct 2025, item 6 (document): Undergraduate discount rate. The committee noted that the first-year institutional discount rate of 47% was above the peer median. Approved: a rebalanced merit scholarship schedule for Fall 2026 entrants, with Presidential awards unchanged; need-based grant policy unchanged. Projected effect: net tuition revenue per first-year +6%. The VP Finance advised that any effect on yield was expected to be small, based on the enrolment consultant's 2021 price-elasticity estimate. Admissions to be informed of the new award amounts before early-action decisions are released.
16	
17	BRIEF:
18	The enrolment drop does not point to the Admissions Office. Applications and admits rose, and applicant quality held steady. Yield, meaning the share of admits who enrolled, fell from 41.8% to 34.3%. The fall is concentrated in the two tiers where merit awards were cut: Dean's went from $14,000 to $9,000 and Merit from $9,000 to $5,000. Their yield fell about 13 points each. Presidential awards and the no-award group were roughly flat. Early-action admits, who got decisions on the old timetable and were unaffected by the portal delay, lost yield as much as regular-decision admits. So the slow portal turnaround does not explain most of the loss, though it was a real service failure that hurt individual students. I can't tell whether the portal lost documents. Replacing the director would punish the wrong party and wouldn't fix the cause. Next step: take the scholarship schedule back to the finance committee with a model of restoring awards in the Dean's and Merit tiers, and the revenue trade-off, before award letters go out. Also set a monthly regular-decision turnaround target. Hold off on the vendor rebuild until the missing-document claim is checked. I'm fairly confident about the scholarship finding; the evidence doesn't isolate the turnaround effect cleanly.
19
